headline: Warsh's Jackson Hole hawkish signal puts a September Fed rate hike back on the table, a headwind for risk assets; geopolitical risk of US-Iran escalation and potential oil supply shock is underappreciated by consensus
reasoning: Bennett sees Kevin Warsh's Jackson Hole comments as firing a shot across the bow for equity investors who assumed no further rate hike risk. He argues that while raising rates is an old-style response to inflation driven by energy costs, institutional pressure at the Fed makes a hike plausible. Separately, he believes Wall Street is underestimating the risk of a larger Middle East war involving the US and Iran, with a potential bombing of Karg Island creating a significant global oil shortage. Both forces are headwinds for the US equity market.
quote: Warsh is also having to deal with the board and a very large and entrenched institution and so regardless of his own thoughts I think there is a lot of pressure there that's simply within the institution if inflation is high in the United States we're showing signs of gaining further traction that they should look to raise interest rates. So he's just fired that shot I guess across the bow of people who were thinking there were no further risks on the interest rate front. That is something for equities to consider because at the same time Besant is trying to intervene in the bond market to keep it afloat.

headline: Long-term bearish on the US dollar, US bonds and potentially US equities due to fiscal profligacy, BRICS withdrawal from Treasuries, and geopolitical risk
reasoning: Bennett cites the US fiscal deficit and money printing as forcing higher borrowing costs, while BRICS nations withdraw from the US Treasury market. Geopolitical tensions raise the risk that China could have its Treasury holdings seized in a conflict scenario, incentivising further diversification away from US bonds. He sees a long-term cyclical decline in the greenback, with periodic buying flurries. Besant's attempt to intervene in the bond market is noted as a sign of stress.
quote: So long term sell the US dollar sell US bonds maybe even sell US stocks and property but we'll see about those. The decline in bond prices higher bond yields has been going on for quite some time. We've been very sure as bonds for a very long time as BRICS nations you know be some of them withdraw quite a bit from the US Treasury market and with these geopolitical tensions rising there's always the threat of a conflict of any kind even a small one between China and the US.

headline: Long-term bullish despite short-term volatility; geopolitical tensions, industrial and jewellery demand support gold even as Warsh's hawkish comments temporarily weigh on price
reasoning: Bennett argues gold should not be sold down on inflation fears alone; it remains a geopolitical hedge against escalating Middle East and Ukraine risks. Long-term demand is supported by industrial and jewellery use as global wealth grows. Short-term buyers may face some losses around conflict events but the long-term case is strong. He distinguishes between the current hawkish Fed signal and what he sees as the correct policy response (rate cuts to fight cost-push inflation).
quote: I'm just basically bullish gold long term for you know reasons of industrial demand and jewelry demand. Everything world is getting wealthy or the world's wealthy are getting wealthy at the wealth gap is growing. So demand for gold is only going to go skywards and I think you need to be long term gold but it could be volatile in the short term around this around conflict. So long term sell the US dollar sell US bonds maybe even sell US stocks and property but we'll see about those and for gold I think if you buy it here you could have some short term loss but over the long term it should really look after you quite well.

headline: Forecasting Australian dollar to reach parity with USD over the next three to four years, driven by Australia's resource wealth and a weakening greenback
reasoning: Bennett is making this call for the second time in his career, having previously forecast parity from 78 cents correctly. The basis is Australia's resource-rich economy being well positioned to benefit from a long-term cyclical decline in the US dollar. He acknowledges the odds are against him repeating this call.
quote: For the second time in my career I'm forecasting the Australian dollar could go to parity to the US dollar over the next three to four years and last time I made that three to four year forecast the Aussie was at 78 cents and it did go to parity over three to four years. So the odds are against me for getting it right twice but I have just made that forecast and that's on the basis that of Australia's resource rich and is positioned to maximize the potential of a weakening greenback.

headline: Cautious on Australian equities: corporate profits still above pre-COVID levels but going sideways to softening since 2022; private sector entering recession masked by public sector expansion
reasoning: Bennett acknowledges that corporate profits are significantly higher than pre-COVID levels, validating prior equity strength, but argues that since 2022 profits have been going sideways to softening. He also flags that Australia's public sector now represents ~26% of GDP, which is masking weakness in the private sector. A Middle East escalation could put the Australian equity market under further pressure, warranting caution.
quote: I think the trend is still much higher profits than existed pre-COVID significantly higher profits across the corporate world than existed pre-COVID and that validates strength in the Australian equity market but probably we've already seen that priced in and I do think since 2022 now corporate profits have been going sideways to softening and that is a concern plus should there be a more significant flare up in the Middle East the Australian equity market could come under pressure again. Well for the Australian economic situation I think private sector is going into recession you know public sector is now a world leading 26% of the economy and that's disguising or softening in the aggregate GDP data just how soft the private sector is.

headline: Clifford Bennett views Kevin Warsh's removal of Fed forward guidance positively, seeing it as a step toward a more credible and modern Federal Reserve
reasoning: Bennett argues the dot plot and forward guidance were unreliable and often embarrassing for the Fed, as external forecasters could predict Fed policy better than the Fed itself. He sees Warsh as a good appointment who will focus more on getting policy right than on managing public perception. He believes this refocusing is positive for the US economy and hopes the RBA might adopt a similar approach.
quote: The forward guidance was really, the dot plot is really a Fed creation and they're removing it and removing some of that guidance is a good idea because it was a little bit embarrassing for the Federal Reserve that people like myself could forecast Federal Reserve monetary policy better than the Federal Reserve could... I think Kevin Walsh is a good selection for the job. He's going to be more of a modern, more of a globalist, I think, Federal Reserve chairman.

headline: Clifford Bennett sees oil overshooting to $60 before recovering to $80 as Middle East supply constraints persist and sovereign demand for strategic reserves rises
reasoning: Bennett argues that oil retreating to pre-war levels isn't justified given the world is still down 9-11% on supply from the Middle East. He expects an overshoot to the downside towards $60 before a recovery to $80, driven by a 6-9 month timeline for Middle East supply to normalise. He also highlights that sovereign demand for strategic reserves will be strong globally, including potential Australian reserves, and that US strategic reserves had fallen ~40% and need rebuilding. This combination of constrained supply and strong sovereign demand supports a recovery after any near-term overshoot.
quote: I think with the oil price, we could see an overshoot towards $60, but then I wouldn't be surprised if the market was surprised and we had a rally back to $80 a barrel, because it's going to be the case going forward that there still is shortages of supply out of the Middle East. A lot of experts are saying it could be six, nine months, something 12, but let's say it's in the six to nine month range before oil supply out of the Middle East has returned to normal. I think the world is down sort of nine to 11% on supply at the moment, but that's still a significant loss. And therefore, oil retreating to where it was before the war isn't quite right, and is that overshoot I was talking about.

headline: Clifford Bennett believes the RBA's next move will be a rate cut, approximately three meetings away, as inflation moderates and the private sector weakens
reasoning: Bennett points to the faster-than-expected fall in oil prices, a modest inflation print, and resilient but not alarming unemployment as reasons for the RBA to hold and ultimately cut. He notes Australia's Q1 GDP print was only 0.3%, signalling a slowing private sector. He argues that oil price weakness could even be deflationary in 6-9 months, removing any justification for further hikes. His base case is no more hikes this year or next, with a rate cut the next likely move around three meetings away.
quote: I think there's no reason for the RBA to hike interest rates again. I mean, I saw at most one more hike, and I thought that was an if, with an equal balance of scenarios for no more hikes, then rate cuts. So I think people need to factor in the next move by the Reserve Bank who will be to reduce rates because of a weakening private sector with inflation not seen to be the greater uncertainty and great risk that it was... I would say the rate cut move is probably three meetings away.

He concludes the next RBA move will be a rate cut, likely three meetings away, as inflation risk is diminishing quickly.

I mean, I saw at most one more hike, and I thought that was an if, with an equal balance of scenarios for no more hikes, then rate cuts. So I think people need to factor in the next move by the Reserve Bank who will be to reduce rates because of a weakening private sector with inflation not seen to be the greater uncertainty and great risk that it was. So I think there's reason, plenty of reason there now for the RBA not to hike rates again at all this year or even next year. And in fact, the next move could be a rate cut. I would say the rate cut move is probably three meetings away.

He also points to strong sovereign demand as countries rebuild strategic reserves — notably the US, whose strategic reserves had fallen ~40%. headline: Clifford Bennett advocates for RBA rate hold at June meeting, arguing domestic economy is fragile and externally-driven inflation is beyond the RBA's control
reasoning: Bennett believes the correct monetary policy response would actually be a rate cut given the private sector is under pressure and the property market is showing vulnerability, but he does not expect the RBA to act that boldly. He argues the RBA faces unprecedented simultaneous domestic and external uncertainty. The geopolitical-driven inflation cannot be influenced by the RBA, so the central bank should focus on supporting the domestic economy. A hold would at least reassure businesses and households. He expects rates to remain on hold at the June meeting.
quote: I can't see them being wise enough to do that. So but if they could be just a little bit wise and keep rates on hold, I think that's the most likely scenario because, I mean, even for the RBA, they must be able to recognize there's never been greater uncertainties around the domestic economy and the external situation at the same time... it's not an inflation the RBA can control or influence. So it should be focused on the other side of the ledger, which is supporting a strong economy and smoothing out the rollercoaster that the RBA has contributed to really since COVID.

headline: Clifford Bennett warns of prolonged Middle East conflict keeping global oil supply 10-12% below pre-war levels through 2026-2027, driving persistent inflationary pressure
reasoning: Bennett argues the US-Iran conflict is a slow-moving but relentless inflationary force, unlike COVID's sudden shock. He notes Iran has fully closed the Strait of Hormuz again following fresh US strikes, with reports of vessels being fired upon. He estimates global oil supply is down 10-12% and expects this reduction to persist through the rest of 2025 and into 2027. He draws a parallel between the nature of US strikes and preparation for potential ground troop deployment or control of the Strait, suggesting a larger strategic plan may be in play. The resulting inflation will be difficult for central banks to control as it is externally driven.
quote: We're now down to only about 10% to 12% of the global oil supply being reduced. But that is still significant, and the world will still go through the economy, the global economy will still go through some pain in adjusting to those lower levels. I'd suggest though that reduction of 10% and more will prevail through the rest of this year and perhaps into 2027. So there is going to be a global economic impact. We've just seen inflation accelerate in the United States, and I think there is going to be more of that. So it's sort of like a, you know, COVID was this sudden tsunami of inflation, whereas in this situation, this geopolitical situation, it's more a tsunami that's just relentless but slow moving.

headline: Clifford Bennett calls for RBA to keep rates on hold given extreme domestic and international uncertainty, while personally preferring a cut
reasoning: Bennett believes the correct monetary policy response is a rate cut given the private sector is under pressure and the property sector is looking vulnerable. However, he expects the RBA will keep rates on hold given the unprecedented combination of domestic economic slowdown and geopolitical-driven inflation externally. He argues the inflation being imported from the Middle East conflict is not something the RBA can control or influence, so it should focus on supporting the domestic economy rather than tightening. He views a hold as the most likely outcome and sees it as a reassuring signal for businesses and households.
quote: I'd like to see her act in a way that she doesn't have to be asked the difficult questions. And that is to keep interest rates where they are. They should be cut like the correct monetary policy response to this type of inflation where the private sector is already on its knees, where the housing sector is suddenly looking a little bit the property sector, a little bit vulnerable. That interest rates should be cut. However, I can't see them being wise enough to do that... I think on hold, they will have to be given the high levels of uncertainty, both domestically and internationally.

headline: Recommends buying post-IPO on any dip, expecting long-term upside despite near-term profit-taking risk
reasoning: Bennett acknowledges the SpaceX IPO is massively oversubscribed and benefits from universal excitement about space, calling it one of the easiest marketing exercises in float history. He expects initial euphoria to be overdone, creating a potential dip buying opportunity a few weeks after the stock begins trading. He acknowledges a risk that SpaceX could immediately take off without pulling back, leaving buyers behind. However, he believes long-term demand from investors who missed out will overwhelm any profit-takers, making it a good long-term buy.
quote: I would certainly be looking to buy the dip after the float, after the initial offering and floating of the stock on the exchange. I think give it a few weeks, see where it's at there. That might even give you a better buying opportunity. That said, there is a risk. There is probably a big risk to that idea. And that is that SpaceX takes off like a rocket... I can't see the profit takers in the long run overwhelming those who will still be left without the stock that they want. So I think, yes, it will be a good long term buy.

headline: Bennett highlights BHP as having performed well and as a preferred resource exposure given geopolitical tailwinds
reasoning: Bennett contrasts BHP favourably against Fortescue, noting BHP has performed well and does not carry the same client concentration risk to China. In a world of resource wars he sees diversified miners like BHP as likely to be well supported over the medium to long term.
quote: Well, you know, BHP's performed really well. Fortescue hasn't performed as well because its major clientele is China. And could there be complications to that? So I think if you have to look at individual stocks within individual countries with a very strong geopolitical lens at the moment.

headline: Bennett flags Fortescue's China-client concentration as a risk relative to BHP in the current geopolitical environment
reasoning: Bennett notes Fortescue has underperformed relative to BHP because its major customer base is China. He raises the question of whether geopolitical complications between the US and China could create further headwinds for Fortescue, suggesting investors apply a strong geopolitical lens when choosing between resource names.
quote: Fortescue hasn't performed as well because its major clientele is China. And could there be complications to that? So I think if you have to look at individual stocks within individual countries with a very strong geopolitical lens at the moment.

headline: Bennett argues resource and AI/robotics companies will become quasi-military assets over a 3–5 year horizon, attracting heavy buying regardless of near-term market volatility
reasoning: Bennett believes the world has entered an era of resource wars where all parties are scrambling to seize resource assets. This makes resource companies strategic military-adjacent holdings that will attract buying from multiple corners of society. He extends the same logic to AI and robotics, citing military implications. He sees these sectors as the most resilient in a sustained geopolitical conflict environment.
quote: I think the impact for the broad stock market would be worse. Now, that's not to say all stocks will be in that sort of degree of trouble. Obviously, these are resource wars. We're going to have resource wars for years to come. Sadly now, I believe the gloves are off for all parties around the world to seize resource assets wherever they can. And that means that resource companies are going to become almost a military asset long term over the three to five-year horizon. So those sorts of stocks are going to be heavily bought from all sorts of corners of interest, if you like, in society. And I also think you have to think about AI and robotics in a similar way.

headline: Clifford Bennett warns ASX200 could fall to 7,200–8,150 if Middle East conflict escalates, with 10–15% probability of full-scale war resumption
reasoning: Bennett assigns a 10–15% probability to a full-scale resumption of war in the Middle East. In that scenario he sees the ASX200 dropping to around 8,150 and the AUD falling toward USD 0.68. If the war drags on one to three months, he sees deeper downside for the ASX200 to 7,500–7,200 and the AUD to 0.65–0.67, driven by fuel shortages and potential recession from energy disruption. He frames this as a risk-management exercise rather than a base case.
quote: I think if we get a resumption of war, now that's, I would say it's only a 10 to 15 percent probability at the moment. But if you're going to manage risk in this high-stakes geopolitical environment, you have to consider all the possibilities and manage your portfolio accordingly. So 10 to 15 percent risk of all-out and even worse war than before, that could drive the Australian market, you know, down to around $8,150, the ASX200, could drive the Australian dollar down towards $0.68. But that's on a resumption of a full-scale war. Should the war last again another one to three months? Then you get downside risk for the Australian dollar of about 10 percent overall, which puts it down at $0.67, $0.65. And the Australian stock market, the ASX200 down at $7,500, maybe $7,200.

headline: Bennett sees Tesla's robotics division as a future military asset likely to attract significant US government investment support
reasoning: Bennett argues Tesla's robotics capabilities have potential military implications and therefore the company will be well supported by massive US government investment at some point. He places Tesla in the same strategic bucket as resource companies — stocks that will prove resilient or outperform in a world of escalating geopolitical competition.
quote: I also think you have to think about AI and robotics in a similar way. I mean, look at someone like Tesla. The robotics there could have military implications going forward, and that will be a company that will be well supported by massive U.S. investment at some point again.

headline: Clifford Bennett recommends hedging portfolios via long oil futures positions as insurance against Middle East conflict escalation
reasoning: Bennett suggests investors can hedge equity portfolios by placing buy orders in oil futures above market price, so that any outbreak of hostilities resulting in a spike in oil prices would generate offsetting profits. He sees this as a practical risk management tool given the binary near-term outcome on Iran.
quote: You can hedge your portfolio by being long oil futures or having orders to buy above the market. So war breaks out and the oil price starts running higher, you're making some profits there to offset.

headline: Clifford Bennett urges caution on macro outlook citing elevated risk of US-Iran conflict escalation and potential oil price spike to $125+
reasoning: Bennett warns that despite Trump's optimistic rhetoric about near-complete negotiations, Iran has publicly stated it will not surrender and has threatened to deploy previously unused weapons systems targeting Gulf State energy infrastructure. He notes oil traders — who have closer Middle East contacts — have not fully priced in a peace deal, with oil prices remaining firm. He believes the situation could resolve either way within days, and recommends investors avoid pre-empting outcomes.
quote: I think it's worth just being a little bit circumspect for a few days... that sort of scenario would really see oil at 125 or even higher.

headline: Clifford Bennett advises against buying Australian equities ahead of Iran-US resolution, but flags aggressive buying opportunity if peace deal confirmed
reasoning: Bennett says he would not be jumping into stocks ahead of clarity on the Iran situation, citing a worrisome budget and rising unemployment (4.5%, highest since 2021) as additional headwinds. However, he notes the Australian market has already priced in a degree of worst-case scenario and would offer more upside than the US market if a peace deal is reached.
quote: If the market breaks up tomorrow because there is a peace deal, I'm going to be one of the most aggressive bulls and buyers of Australian stocks because they have priced in a worst case scenario to some degree already.
